forces.title: Data Centre Buildout Boosts Activity
forces.description: Significant data centre buildout is expected to drive activity in Norway, benefiting related industries and contributing to overall economic growth. This buildout represents a direct increase in demand for Data Centre Real Estate, driven by growing computational needs from artificial intelligence and other digital transformation efforts, supporting development and investment.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 3/2026: Minor changes in growth prospects

forces.title: Data Centre Investment Accelerating in Norway
forces.description: Firms in Norway are planning increased investment in 2026 and 2027, with data centre buildout identified as a primary driver. This trend is not only lifting activity among service contacts in the short term but is also expected to accelerate growth further in 2027, indicating sustained and expanding demand for data centre real estate development and related infrastructure.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 3/2026: Minor changes in growth prospects

forces.title: AI Compute and Electrification Drive Data Centre Demand
forces.description: The expansion of AI compute and electrification initiatives globally is creating substantial demand for data centers. This includes requirements for components like steel and rare-earth magnets, cooling systems, and power solutions, indicating robust growth for data centre real estate as these foundational technologies are built out. This trend, measured in the US, reflects a global imperative applicable to Europe.
forces.source_title: Winning America’s Reindustrialization

forces.title: Supply Chain Bottlenecks Hinder Data Centre Development
forces.description: Global supply chains for critical components at the intersection of AI compute and power, such as electric-grade silicon steel and liquid-cooling systems, face long lead times and multiyear backlogs. These constraints pose a significant risk to the speed and cost-effectiveness of data centre development and expansion, including in Europe, potentially delaying new capacity coming online and increasing project costs.
forces.source_title: Winning America’s Reindustrialization

forces.title: Rising Construction Costs Impede New Industrial Capacity
forces.description: Rapid growth in nonresidential construction costs, combined with lengthy permitting timelines, litigation risks, and labor/equipment shortages, significantly increases the hurdle rate for developing new industrial and logistics facilities. This cost pressure acts as a headwind, making new build-outs of industrial estates and Grade A warehousing more expensive and challenging to justify economically across Europe, impacting project feasibility.
forces.source_title: Winning America’s Reindustrialization

forces.title: Value Chain Localization Boosts Domestic Industrial Real Estate Demand
forces.description: A global trend towards localizing value chains, driven by geopolitical tensions, supply chain risks, and a desire for speed and quality, encourages manufacturers to produce goods closer to domestic customers. This shift is expected to increase demand for industrial estates and warehousing facilities within Europe, as companies prioritize resilient regional footprints over low-cost foreign production models.
forces.source_title: Winning America’s Reindustrialization

forces.title: Geopolitical Tensions Threaten AI Compute Supply Chain
forces.description: High concentration of critical AI compute components, like leading-edge chips and rare-earth magnets, in regions vulnerable to geopolitical tensions (e.g., Taiwan, Mainland China) poses a significant risk. Disruptions in these supply chains could directly impact the development and operational continuity of data centers in Europe, which rely on these inputs, affecting both construction timelines and hardware availability.
forces.source_title: Winning America’s Reindustrialization

forces.title: Terrestrial Data Centres Face Land and Power Constraints
forces.description: Data centers globally are encountering increasing limitations regarding available land and power supply, which hampers their expansion and development. These mounting constraints represent a significant headwind for traditional terrestrial data centre real estate, prompting exploration of alternative solutions like space-based data centers, and challenging the growth of physical facilities in Europe.
forces.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

forces.title: Cooling Systems Remain Major Data Centre Bottleneck
forces.description: Effective cooling remains a significant technical bottleneck for large-scale data centre deployment, particularly for advanced architectures like space-based systems. This challenge highlights the ongoing need for innovative and efficient cooling solutions in terrestrial data centres in Europe to manage increasing heat emissions from high-density AI workloads, presenting a hurdle for operational scalability and efficiency improvements.
forces.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

forces.title: Real-Time AI Workloads Anchor Terrestrial Data Centre Demand
forces.description: AI applications requiring real-time responsiveness, such as interactive AI assistants and autonomous systems, are inherently better suited for terrestrial data centre infrastructure due to unavoidable communication delays in low-Earth orbit. Additionally, training large foundation models demands tightly coupled compute clusters and high power densities that orbital systems cannot match, ensuring continued strong demand for terrestrial facilities.
forces.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

forces.title: Hyperscalers Drive Robust Data Centre Demand and Investment
forces.description: Well-capitalized hyperscalers are anchoring demand for data centers globally, demonstrating approximately 50 percent annual capital spending growth from 2022 to 2026 while maintaining strong financial health. Their committed, durable growth underpins sustained demand for data centre real estate, including in Europe, indicating a strong foundation for future development and capacity utilization across the sector.
forces.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

forces.title: Macro and Geopolitical Factors Threaten Data Centre Buildout Pace
forces.description: Broader macro and geopolitical factors, including tighter capital markets, elevated power prices, and supply chain disruptions, pose significant risks that could dampen demand and slow the pace of data centre buildout. These external pressures introduce uncertainty for data centre real estate development in Europe, potentially impacting investment and expansion timelines and increasing project costs.
forces.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

forces.title: Community Opposition Restricts Data Centre Development
forces.description: Growing community pushback against data centre development is emerging as a significant force restricting new projects. This opposition can lead to project postponements and cancellations, directly impacting the availability of suitable sites and increasing regulatory hurdles for data centre real estate in Europe, thereby slowing capacity expansion and development timelines, as seen with 4 GW of projects postponed in Q1 2026 in the US.
forces.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

forces.title: Speculative Interconnection Requests Distort Data Centre Demand
forces.description: A massive backlog of speculative and duplicative load interconnection pipeline requests for data centers distorts true demand estimates. Developers often submit multiple requests or secure rights without firm projects, creating a misleading impression of demand. This practice complicates utility planning and can lead to misallocation of capital in data centre real estate, posing a risk of overestimation in European markets and affecting infrastructure build-out.
forces.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

forces.title: Utility Measures Counter Speculative Data Centre Power Requests
forces.description: Utilities are implementing new policies, such as large-load tariffs and increased down payments, to curb speculative power interconnection requests and encourage credible data centre projects. This structural change aims to streamline demand signals, reduce stranded cost risks, and improve planning accuracy for power infrastructure. It will impact how data centre developers approach securing power in European markets, fostering more serious commitments.
forces.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

forces.title: Data Centres Shift Towards Permanent On-Site Power Generation
forces.description: Data centre operators are increasingly deploying permanent on-site power and management solutions, including gas engines, turbines, fuel cells, and battery storage. This shift is driven by critical system uptime requirements, resilience concerns, and the need for faster market entry due to grid constraints. This structural change redefines the power supply model for data centre real estate in Europe, impacting location and design decisions.
forces.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

forces.title: Data Centres Transition to 800-Volt DC for Higher Efficiency
forces.description: Driven by increasing energy demands from AI models, data centers are transitioning to higher-voltage power architectures, specifically 800-volt DC systems. This structural shift aims to reduce electricity conversion losses, manage heat emissions, and simplify power distribution, creating opportunities for specialized component providers and impacting the design and infrastructure requirements for future data centre real estate in Europe.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: Rising Rack Power Density Demands New Data Centre Designs
forces.description: The electricity needs per data centre rack are rapidly increasing, from under 50 kilowatts to 200-600 kilowatts, with projections reaching one megawatt per rack later this decade. This surge in rack power density necessitates a fundamental redesign of data centre infrastructure, including cooling and power distribution, pushing for advanced architectures like 800 VDC to support future AI workloads in European facilities.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: Long Lead Times for Transformers Drive 800 VDC Adoption
forces.description: Extended lead times for conventional transformers, often spanning several years in constrained markets, are strengthening the business case for adopting 800 VDC architectures in data centers. This supply chain bottleneck acts as an incentive for new builds and retrofits to move towards more efficient and readily available 800 VDC solutions, potentially accelerating their deployment in European data centre real estate.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: SSTs Enable Fully DC-Native Greenfield Data Centres
forces.description: Solid-state transformers (SSTs) are expected to accelerate the shift towards fully DC-native data centers, particularly for greenfield AI campuses. By enabling designs built around a high-voltage DC backbone from the outset, SSTs offer a significant upside opportunity to develop highly efficient, scalable, and cost-effective data centre real estate in Europe, driving innovation in new construction and long-term operational savings.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: Higher Rack Densities Force Power-Cooling System Integration
forces.description: The continuous increase in rack power densities within data centers is driving a demand for tighter integration between power and cooling systems. This structural change encourages collaboration across original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and will lead to more holistic design approaches for data centre real estate in Europe, moving towards integrated power and cooling solutions to manage intense heat loads efficiently.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: 800 VDC Safety Concerns Pose Adoption Barrier
forces.description: The transition to 800 VDC systems in data centers introduces new safety challenges, including different shock, fault, and arc flash risks compared to traditional 48-volt rack power. Addressing these concerns requires developing new protection strategies, operating procedures, and workforce training, acting as a primary barrier to rapid, widespread adoption of advanced power architectures in European data centre real estate.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: Lack of Standardisation Slows 800 VDC Data Centre Adoption
forces.description: The absence of mature industry standards for testing methods, equipment requirements, and installation guidelines for 800 VDC data centers presents a significant headwind to their broader adoption. This lack of standardization increases uncertainty and complexity for developers and operators in Europe, hindering the rapid scaling and commercial viability of new power architectures in data centre real estate until clear guidelines emerge.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: Geopolitical Tensions & Trade Uncertainty Dampen Logistics Real Estate Demand
forces.description: Geopolitical tensions are increasing uncertainty in international trade, which directly impacts demand for logistics real estate. This global volatility translates into cautious investor sentiment and can lead to reduced acquisition activity and higher vacancy rates, particularly outside prime locations, posing a significant headwind for logistics real estate development and investment in the Netherlands and wider Europe.
forces.source_title: Recovery in Dutch commercial real estate is less robust than it appears

forces.title: Strategic Location Sustains Dutch Logistics Real Estate Attractiveness
forces.description: The Netherlands' strategic geographical location and its established role as a key transit hub continue to underpin the attractiveness of its logistics real estate market. This inherent advantage acts as a tailwind, supporting underlying demand despite broader market uncertainties, and positioning the country favorably for logistics investment, particularly for well-located, scalable assets with adequate charging infrastructure and efficient operations.
forces.source_title: Recovery in Dutch commercial real estate is less robust than it appears

forces.title: Electrification Demands Shape Logistics Real Estate Investment Decisions
forces.description: The energy transition is driving logistics players towards electrification, making the availability of sufficient charging infrastructure a critical factor in investment and location decisions for logistics real estate. This structural change favors larger, well-located assets with existing or planned charging capabilities, compelling developers and investors in Europe to integrate electrification needs into their strategies to maintain competitiveness and support efficient operations.
forces.source_title: Recovery in Dutch commercial real estate is less robust than it appears

viewpoints.title: Data Centre Buildout Driving Growth in Norwegian Economy
viewpoints.description: Norges Bank's Regional Network contacts anticipate moderate output growth through H2 2026, with data centre buildout identified as a key driver. This indicates a positive outlook for Data Centre Real Estate in Norway, contributing to broader economic activity. The growth is also supported by improved household purchasing power and increased defence spending, signifying a robust demand environment for this asset class.
viewpoints.source_title: Regional Network report 3/2026: Minor changes in growth prospects

viewpoints.title: Terrestrial Data Centres Remain Cost-Competitive Despite Space-Based Emergence
viewpoints.description: BCG Global asserts that while space-based data centers may achieve technical feasibility within 5-10 years, they are unlikely to surpass terrestrial infrastructure on cost, retaining a significant cost premium (1.5x under realistic improvements). Space-based solutions are seen as a complementary layer for specific AI workloads, not a replacement, indicating terrestrial data centers will remain foundational due to their inherent cost advantage.
viewpoints.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

viewpoints.title: Near-Term Investment in Terrestrial AI Infrastructure Recommended
viewpoints.description: BCG Global advises business leaders to continue investing in terrestrial AI infrastructure, emphasizing that space-based data centers are unlikely to achieve cost parity within the decade and the displacement narrative is exaggerated. This reinforces a positive outlook for traditional data centre real estate, suggesting that near-term buildouts of physical facilities remain a sound strategic approach for AI compute needs in Europe.
viewpoints.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

viewpoints.title: Data Centre Capacity Overbuilding Risk Unlikely Despite High Demand
viewpoints.description: McKinsey's analysis suggests that the risk of overbuilding data centre capacity to support AI compute demand is unlikely to materialize, even with escalating forecasts and significant investment in power infrastructure. They indicate that for the power sector, underbuilding capacity might be a greater near-term risk. This provides a cautious-positive outlook for data centre real estate in Europe, implying sustained demand rather than market saturation.
viewpoints.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

viewpoints.title: Power Access Emerging as Data Centre's Scarcest Resource
viewpoints.description: McKinsey suggests that access to reliable power, rather than compute capacity itself, is becoming the scarcest resource for data centers. This perspective implies that future data centre investments, including in Europe, will prioritize sites with robust and scalable power solutions. This outlook underscores the critical importance of power infrastructure for data centre real estate development, making it a primary determinant of viability and value.
viewpoints.source_title: Powering AI: How real is the risk of overbuilding?

viewpoints.title: Dutch Commercial Real Estate Recovery Momentum Fragile
viewpoints.description: ING Think assesses the recovery in the Dutch commercial real estate market as less robust than initial Q1 2026 investment volumes suggest. While investment was up over 60% year-on-year, growth is expected to slow in H2 2026 due to heightened geopolitical uncertainty, rising construction costs, and decreased profitability of new-build projects. This indicates a cautious outlook for the broader commercial real estate sector, including logistics.
viewpoints.source_title: Recovery in Dutch commercial real estate is less robust than it appears

viewpoints.title: Dutch Logistics Real Estate Investors More Cautious Amid Rising Vacancies
viewpoints.description: ING Think observes increased caution among investors in the Dutch logistics real estate market, with rising vacancy rates outside prime locations and heightened geopolitical tensions impacting international trade. This directly affects demand for logistics real estate, leading to a cautious outlook for the sector, particularly for non-prime assets, as investors become more selective in their acquisitions.
viewpoints.source_title: Recovery in Dutch commercial real estate is less robust than it appears

demand_drivers.description: Need to process nationally sensitive data without crossing foreign networks/jurisdictions.
Co-location of compute with data source in orbit for applications like Earth observation.
AI applications not requiring near-real-time response, allowing compute to shift to orbit.

new_opportunities.description: Space-based data centers will serve specific, orbit-advantaged AI workloads, creating a new market segment for computing infrastructure, rather than replacing terrestrial facilities entirely.

market_sizing.methodology: BCG Global estimates that orbit-advantaged use cases could allow space-based data centers to capture 10% to 15% of the global AI data center market by 2040. This implies a potential diversion of a small but strategically important portion of future AI data center demand away from terrestrial facilities.
market_sizing.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

demand_drivers.description: Terrestrial data centers offer a significantly lower total cost of ownership compared to emerging space-based alternatives, maintaining their appeal for most AI workloads.

market_sizing.methodology: BCG Global estimates the 20-year Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) for terrestrial AI data centers to be approximately $230 million to $300 million per MW. This is compared to space-based data centers, which currently carry a 2.5x to 3x cost premium, indicating terrestrial facilities remain significantly more cost-effective.
market_sizing.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

demand_drivers.description: Processing sensitive national data without foreign network transit.
Co-locating compute with in-orbit data sources for immediate analysis.
AI applications where real-time response isn't critical, allowing orbital compute.

new_opportunities.description: Space-based data centers create a new segment for AI workloads with specific needs (e.g., data sovereignty, co-location with data source) that terrestrial infrastructure may not optimally serve.

market_sizing.methodology: BCG Global projects that space-based data centers could generate $240 billion to $320 billion in annual revenue by 2040 by capturing 10% to 15% of the global AI data center market. This revenue potential, driven by orbit-advantaged workloads, represents a competitive element for terrestrial data centers, indicating a segment of AI compute demand may migrate to space.
market_sizing.source_title: Space-Based Data Centers: More Than Hype, but Not a Revolution

pnl_drivers.description: Native 800 VDC systems can cut non-IT infrastructure CapEx by 15-18%, lowering initial investment costs for data centre real estate.
Power-related OpEx can decrease by 8-10% with 800 VDC architectures, improving long-term profitability and operational efficiency for data centers.

market_sizing.methodology: McKinsey estimates that native 800 VDC systems could reduce capital expenditures on non-IT infrastructure for data centers by approximately 15% to 18% and power-related operating expenditures by 8% to 10%. These savings improve the economic viability and efficiency of data centre real estate developments.
market_sizing.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers
